summary:
Visitors in Hauts-de-France stand under France's national framework: criminal law, identity-document rules, anti-discrimination law and marriage law apply uniformly across the region, and the country's oversight bodies record the same pattern of risk everywhere.

Prison placement is the region's documented contact point with trans-visitor risk. Under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender inscribed on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities. Controller-general Adeline Hazan, the national detention inspector-general, identifies transgender detainees as the group that suffers the most in prison.

The BuzzFeed News investigation of 12 January 2018 documents that practice in the region directly. Paola, transferred in 2014 to the correctional facility at Lille, was met by detainees shouting that they did not want any women there, was attacked with a knife by a fellow inmate, and spent two days in solitary confinement. The same investigation records Kara B. held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 protest trial in the capital, and the Ministry of Justice counted 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

The national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 covering every place of deprivation of liberty and built from referrals received since 2010 concerning transgender detainees. It finds that assignment to establishments or wards, male or female, is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and that search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation.

That opinion recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, and urges research funding. It faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules, and the CGLPL issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty after concluding that its 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement.

Placement remained current practice in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October; her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, and placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline is the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The risks concentrate in two settings, detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, France's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition, and the Défenseur des droits frames the problem as violations of fundamental rights rather than criminal liability.

Prison treatment varies between establishments even though placement follows a single documentary rule, so two trans women held in the same period can face materially different conditions. Accounts collected in the BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements, and the CGLPL's findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people identifying structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

The 2016 legal gender-recognition reform did not change custodial practice: the CGLPL recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion, and the national preventive mechanism told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the earlier one produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees.

France's position sits within an EU measurement frame: the Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey supplies the comparative discrimination figure cited by the Défenseur des droits, rather than a national French survey.
localsOnly:
Residents held in places of deprivation of liberty can invoke the CGLPL's 25 May 2021 recommendations: choice of the sex of searching officers and of ward, no isolation on the basis of identity, continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, and the administration's obligation to translate the 2016 justice-modernisation law into prison rules.

The 2016 gender-recognition reform governs legal recognition for residents, and the oversight framework now expressly covers intersex and non-binary detainees as well as trans detainees.

Residents discriminated against in services have guidance on their side: the Défenseur des droits' framework decision on trans rights sets out official instructions for service providers and is grounded in case files and association testimony.

Same-sex marriage has been available since the 2013 law, giving residents a settled route to partner recognition.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory gives a count of transgender detainees in Hauts-de-France facilities, or for the region's prisons after the Ministry of Justice figure of 13 detainees across eight facilities nationally as of 1 November 2016. That figure is national and dated; a current regional count is not sourced here.

Whether the CGLPL's binding guidance of 25 May 2021 has been implemented at the correctional facility at Lille is unresolved in the sources. The opinion records that the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement; no post-2021 compliance assessment is available.

The outcome of oral question no. 219 concerning Louna's placement at Tarbes is not sourced, and whether she remains in isolation is unresolved.

The inventory contains no region-specific data on hate-crime reporting, on police treatment of trans people outside border settings, or on access to gender-affirming care in Hauts-de-France. The 64% discrimination figure is national, drawn from an EU-wide 2023 survey, and is not broken down by region.

Whether the Défenseur des droits' framework decision carries binding force against service providers, as opposed to guidance, is not stated in the sources.
